 SME Ministry analyzes three years of LIPS results
765 small businesses attracted investment; 10 grew into mid-sized companies
Revenue rose 43%, employment 31%; export markets expanded from 32 to 57
 The Ministry of SMEs and Startups on the 30th released its “Analysis of Private Investment Trends in Small Businesses Engaged in Local Startups.” Since the introduction of LIPS in 2023, 765 small businesses engaged in local startups have attracted 122.7 billion won in private investment, and 10 of them have grown into mid-sized companies. The beneficiary companies’ average revenue rose 43%, from 770 million won to 1.09 billion won, while average employment increased 31%, from 4.0 to 5.3 people. Fifty-one companies attracted a total of 39.2 billion won in follow-on investment. The share of companies exporting rose from 12.0% to 22.7%, and the number of export markets expanded from 32 to 57. Korean consumer goods, including cosmetics (45.1% of export value), drove exports. The ministry will hold a LIPS results-sharing event in conjunction with the first Local Startup Festival, scheduled for Nov. 4-6 in Jeju.
 Local_startup_LIPS_results_infographic.jpg A skincare brand in Seoul’s Guro district has grown revenue from 4 billion won to 26 billion won in three years and now sells its products in 40 countries. A decaffeinated coffee bean company in Paju boosted revenue 154% in a year through exclusive supply deals with a major coffee franchise. And a Jeju restaurant specializing in black goat has become a mid-sized company with Korea’s only “black goat momguk.” What these three companies have in common is that they used LIPS , which links private investment with government support, as a springboard.
 The Ministry of SMEs and Startups (MSS) on the 30th released its “Analysis of Private Investment Trends in Small Businesses Engaged in Local Startups.” Since the program was introduced in 2023, 765 local startup small businesses have received a total of 122.7 billion won in private investment through LIPS.
 Three businesses transformed by LIPS: On:greedients, Vinspece and Andamiro Neulbom
 The ministry’s featured examples offer a snapshot of how local startups can grow.
 Power Player (selected in 2023; Guro, Seoul) operates the skincare brand On:greedients and focused its LIPS loan support on developing sales channels. The company has sold $4.44 million worth of products in about 40 countries, from Asian markets including China and Japan to North America. Revenue surged for three consecutive years, rising from 4.08 billion won in 2023 to 26.08 billion won in 2025, and the company entered the mid-sized category. After joining LIPS, it also secured 2 billion won in follow-on investment from CJ ENM and is now pursuing expansion beyond skincare into color cosmetics.
 Vinspece (selected in 2025; Paju, Gyeonggi Province) imports, distributes and processes green coffee beans for decaffeinated coffee. It invested commercialization funds in product development, creating and launching two flavored decaf coffee stick products, and secured an exclusive supply deal with a major coffee franchise. Revenue grew 154%, from 12.6 billion won in 2024 to 31.5 billion won in 2025, while employment rose 142.9%.
 Andamiro Neulbom (selected in 2023; Jeju) specializes in black goat. It invested loan support in expanding its business, developing differentiated new products including Korea’s only “black goat momguk” and black goat extract. After three consecutive years of revenue growth—from 2 billion won in 2023 to 2.9 billion won in 2025—it became a mid-sized company and successfully opened a second location.
 How LIPS works: Private investors invest first, then the government matches the funding
 LIPS (Local & Lifestyle biz Incubator Program for Strong SME) is a program in which private investment firms designated as operators by the MSS first invest in small businesses engaged in local startups that draw on distinctive local resources, culture and characteristics. The ministry then provides matching support through policy loans and commercialization funds. Small businesses that attract private investment can receive loans of up to five times their investment, capped at 500 million won, and commercialization funding of up to three times their investment, capped at 200 million won.
 Investment has grown year by year. Average cumulative investment per company rose from 117 million won in 2023 to 160 million won in 2026, while the share of companies receiving an initial investment of at least 100 million won increased from 43.0% to 57.9%. Manufacturing accounted for the largest share by industry, with 321 companies, or 42%, followed by services (17%), information and communications (16%) and wholesale and retail (16%). Unlike venture capital, which focuses on technology, investment in local startups is spreading across businesses rooted in everyday life, from consumer-goods manufacturing such as food and beauty products to lifestyle services and education and talent-matching platforms.
 The age of business founders also stands out. Young founders in their 20s and 30s accounted for 42.9% of business leaders—5.6 times the 7.7% share among all small businesses, according to the 2024 Small Business Survey.
 Results: Revenue up 43%, employment up 31%; 70.7% are high-growth companies
 Average revenue per local startup small business that attracted private investment rose 43%, from 765 million won before receiving support to 1.094 billion won, while average employment increased 31%, from 4.0 to 5.3 people. These companies added a total of 646 jobs. High-growth companies, defined as those with revenue growth of at least 20% over three years, accounted for 70.7%, and 51 companies attracted a total of 39.2 billion won in follow-on investment. Early-stage companies with three years or less of operating history posted particularly strong increases of 188% in revenue and 100% in employment.
 The program also had an impact on regional economies. A total of 298 companies outside the capital region—38.9% of all recipients—attracted 58.27 billion won, or 47.5% of total investment. Manufacturing accounted for a larger share outside the capital region (49.7%) than within it (37%), suggesting that private-sector interest in small businesses with local manufacturing bases is translating into investment.
 Korean consumer goods drive exports, with cosmetics accounting for 45% of export value
 Exports also expanded. The share of companies exporting rose from 12.0% in 2023 to 22.7% in 2025, while average exports per company increased from 183 million won to 233 million won. Cosmetics led exports at 11.7 billion won, or 45.1% of the total, followed by apparel at 2.9 billion won, or 11.1%. The top export destinations by number of companies were the United States (49), Japan (40) and China (37). The number of export markets grew from 32 to 57, pointing to diversification into Europe, the Middle East and other regions.
 Meanwhile, the MSS will hold the “2026 LIPS Results-Sharing Event” in conjunction with the first Local Startup Festival in Jeju, scheduled for Nov. 4-6. The event will highlight investment results and successful growth cases among local startups, and recognize this year’s LIPS operators and small businesses.
 Kim Jung-joo, the MSS director general for small business policy, said, “As global demand for Korean consumer goods grows, local startups are showing clear growth and emerging as attractive investment targets. The ministry will continue to expand private investment opportunities for promising local small businesses, support their growth and add vitality to regional economies.”
